code.title: Turnaround, waiting and response time: FCFS vs Round Robin
code.python:
# Turnaround, waiting and response time for FCFS vs Round Robin
procs = [("P1", 0, 8), ("P2", 1, 4), ("P3", 2, 2)]  # name, arrival, burst

def fcfs(ps):
    t, out = 0, {}
    for n, at, bt in sorted(ps, key=lambda p: p[1]):
        t = max(t, at)
        out[n] = (t, t + bt)  # first run, completion
        t += bt
    return out

def rr(ps, q):
    rem = {n: bt for n, at, bt in ps}
    first, done, queue, t, i = {}, {}, [], 0, 0
    ps = sorted(ps, key=lambda p: p[1])
    while len(done) < len(ps):
        while i < len(ps) and ps[i][1] <= t:   # admit arrivals
            queue.append(ps[i][0]); i += 1
        if not queue:
            t = ps[i][1]; continue
        n = queue.pop(0)
        first.setdefault(n, t)
        run = min(q, rem[n]); t += run; rem[n] -= run
        while i < len(ps) and ps[i][1] <= t:   # arrivals during the slice go first
            queue.append(ps[i][0]); i += 1
        if rem[n] > 0: queue.append(n)
        else: done[n] = t
    return {n: (first[n], done[n]) for n in done}

def report(title, res):
    print(title)
    tot = [0, 0, 0]
    for n, at, bt in procs:
        fr, ct = res[n]
        tat, wt, rt = ct - at, ct - at - bt, fr - at
        print(f"  {n}: TAT={tat} WT={wt} RT={rt}")
        tot = [tot[0] + tat, tot[1] + wt, tot[2] + rt]
    print("  avg TAT=%.2f WT=%.2f RT=%.2f" % tuple(x / len(procs) for x in tot))

print("processes (name, arrival, burst):", procs)
report("FCFS", fcfs(procs))
report("Round Robin q=2", rr(procs, 2))

followUps: Round Robin with a very small quantum is good at response time but bad at turnaround. Every job gets the CPU within one cycle of the queue, so the first run happens quickly, but every job is chopped into many pieces and finishes late. Example: three jobs of 10 units each, q=1: each job first runs by time 2, yet they finish at 28, 29 and 30 (average 29). Run one after another (FCFS) they finish at 10, 20, 30 (average 20) but the last one waits 20 for its first run. Add context switch costs and the gap grows.

CPU utilization is the percentage of time the CPU is doing useful work, and it can be low even with many processes if most of them are blocked, not ready. If 10 processes each need the CPU 10% of the time and wait on disk or network for the other 90%, they often all wait together and the CPU sits idle. With a fraction p of time spent waiting, n processes give roughly 1 - p^n utilization when waits are independent, so p=0.9, n=10 gives about 65%. Other causes are a convoy behind a slow I/O job, lock contention, or too few threads for the cores.

code.title: Convoy effect: long job first vs short first vs time slicing

followUps: Node.js avoids the convoy by never letting long work sit on the event loop: it moves heavy work off the single JavaScript thread or splits it up. Options are worker_threads or child processes for CPU-bound code, the libuv thread pool for file and crypto calls, and chunking a loop with setImmediate so other callbacks run between chunks. Example: summing 100 million numbers in one handler blocks every request for maybe 100 ms; in 100 chunks of 1 million, other requests get a turn every ~1 ms. It is cooperative scheduling, so the program must yield by itself.

MLFQ puts every new job in the top queue with a short quantum, so short jobs finish there quickly. A job that uses its whole quantum looks CPU-bound and is demoted to a lower queue with longer quanta, while jobs that block early stay high. The scheduler therefore learns burst lengths from past behaviour, with no prior knowledge. Example: a 24-unit hog is demoted after 2 units, so 3-unit jobs arriving later still run at the top level and wait about 2, not 24. A periodic boost stops starvation of the demoted hog.

code.title: SJF exchange argument and exponential burst prediction
code.python:
# SJF exchange argument and exponential averaging of burst predictions
from itertools import permutations

bursts = [6, 8, 7, 3]
def avg_wait(order):
    t = total = 0
    for b in order:
        total += t; t += b
    return total / len(order)

best = min(permutations(bursts), key=avg_wait)
print("bursts:", bursts)
print("best order over all permutations:", best, "avg wait", avg_wait(best))
print("sorted (SJF) order:", tuple(sorted(bursts)), "avg wait", avg_wait(sorted(bursts)))

# tau_next = alpha * actual + (1 - alpha) * tau_prev
alpha, tau = 0.5, 10.0
actual = [6, 4, 6, 4, 13, 13, 13]
print("\nprediction with alpha =", alpha)
for a in actual:
    print(f"  predicted {tau:6.2f}  actual {a}")
    tau = alpha * a + (1 - alpha) * tau
print("  next prediction %.2f" % tau)

followUps: The formula is tau(n+1) = alpha * t(n) + (1 - alpha) * tau(n), where t(n) is the real last CPU burst and tau(n) the previous prediction. Alpha between 0 and 1 sets how much you trust recent behaviour. With alpha=0 the prediction never changes; with alpha=1 it equals the last burst only. Alpha=0.5 is common. Example: tau=10, last burst 6 gives 0.5*6 + 0.5*10 = 8. Unrolled, older bursts get weights (1-alpha)^k, so their influence decays exponentially. Each update costs O(1) time and one stored number per process.

No, SJF is optimal for average waiting time but not fair: a long job can wait forever if short jobs keep arriving. Example: a 100 ms job and a new 1 ms job arriving every ms; the 100 ms job never gets picked. Fairness in the sense of bounded waiting needs aging (raise priority of waiting jobs) or a hybrid like MLFQ. It is also unfair in the sense that short jobs are always favoured; that is what makes the average small, so there is a direct trade-off between average wait and worst-case wait.

code.title: Round Robin: how the quantum affects response and overhead
code.python:
# Round Robin: effect of the time quantum on response and switch overhead
bursts = [10, 10, 10, 10]   # four CPU-bound jobs arriving at 0
switch = 1                  # cost of one context switch

def simulate(q):
    rem, t, first, finish, switches = bursts[:], 0, {}, {}, 0
    while any(rem):
        for i in range(len(rem)):
            if rem[i]:
                first.setdefault(i, t)
                run = min(q, rem[i]); t += run; rem[i] -= run
                if not rem[i]: finish[i] = t
                t += switch; switches += 1   # pay for switching away
    return sum(first.values()) / len(bursts), sum(finish.values()) / len(bursts), switches

print("bursts", bursts, "switch cost", switch)
print("quantum  avg-response  avg-turnaround  switches")
for q in (1, 2, 5, 10, 40):
    r, t, s = simulate(q)
    print(f"{q:7d}  {r:12.1f}  {t:14.1f}  {s:8d}")
print("overhead share at q=2: %.0f%%" % (100 * switch / (2 + switch)))

followUps: It depends on the convention you choose, so you must state it. The common textbook rule is that a newly arriving process enters the queue before the preempted process is put back. Example: q=2, P1 runs 0-2 and P2 arrives at 2 with P1 still needing time; queue becomes P2, P1, so P2 runs next. The opposite rule (preempted process first) gives P1, P2 and P1 runs again. Both are valid and give different Gantt charts and averages, so exams usually say which one to use. If nothing is stated, write down your assumption.

Linux does not use a fixed quantum for normal tasks. Under CFS the slice is the scheduling period times the task's weight share. The period is about 6 ms for few tasks (sched_latency) and grows when there are many, so that each task gets at least a minimum granularity (about 0.75 ms). Example: period 6 ms with two equal tasks gives 3 ms each; with 8 tasks the period stretches to 8 * 0.75 = 6 ms so each gets 0.75 ms. EEVDF in Linux 6.6 and later uses a base slice (about 3 ms) and chooses by virtual deadline. Real-time round robin tasks use a fixed 100 ms default.

code.title: Starvation with priorities and aging as the fix

followUps: Priority inversion is when a high-priority task is effectively delayed by a lower-priority one, usually because the low task holds a lock the high one needs and a medium task prevents the low one from finishing. Mars Pathfinder (1997): the bus management task (high) needed a mutex held by the weather task (low), while a medium communications task kept running. A watchdog saw the bus task miss its deadline and reset the system repeatedly. The fix, enabling priority inheritance on the mutex, was uploaded from Earth. It is a lock problem, not a starvation problem.

No, plain round robin never starves anyone, because every ready process is in the FIFO queue and gets a turn within (n-1) quanta. Example: 5 processes and q=10 ms means any process waits at most 40 ms before running again. Starvation needs a rule that can keep favouring others forever, such as strict priorities or shortest-job-first. Round robin with priorities per level can still starve the low levels unless the levels are time-sliced or aged.

code.title: Tiny multilevel feedback queue with demotion and boost
code.python:
# Tiny MLFQ: 3 levels, quanta 2/4/8, demote on full quantum, periodic boost
quanta = [2, 4, 8]
jobs = {"cpu": 20, "io": 6}      # remaining CPU needed
io_yields = {"io": 1}            # "io" gives up the CPU after 1 unit each turn
queues = [["cpu", "io"], [], []]
t, boost_every, log = 0, 16, []
while any(queues):
    lvl = next(i for i, q in enumerate(queues) if q)
    n = queues[lvl].pop(0)
    # the I/O-bound job blocks early so it uses less than the quantum
    run = min(quanta[lvl], jobs[n], io_yields.get(n, 99))
    jobs[n] -= run
    log.append(f"t={t:2d} {n:3s} L{lvl} ran {run}")
    t += run
    if jobs[n] > 0:
        used_full = run == quanta[lvl]
        dest = min(lvl + 1, 2) if used_full else lvl   # demote only if quantum used up
        queues[dest].append(n)
    if t // boost_every != (t - run) // boost_every:     # periodic priority boost
        for q in queues[1:]:
            queues[0].extend(q); q.clear()
        log.append(f"t={t:2d} BOOST all jobs to L0")
print("\n".join(log))

followUps: A program can game MLFQ by yielding just before its quantum ends, for example doing a tiny I/O every 1 ms of a 2 ms quantum. The scheduler thinks it is interactive and keeps it at the top, so it takes most of the CPU. The fix is to account for total CPU used at a level, not per turn: give each level an allotment (say 10 ms) and demote when it is spent, no matter how often the job blocks. With that rule the gamer is demoted after 10 ms of CPU. The periodic boost also resets any unlucky classification.

Linux replaced the heuristic interactivity detection (the O(1) scheduler with its sleep-time bonuses) with CFS in 2.6.23, and CFS with EEVDF in 6.6. Both use weights and a virtual-time measure instead of queues and guessed priorities. A task that sleeps a lot automatically has a small vruntime or positive lag, so it runs soon after waking, which gives the MLFQ benefit without heuristics. Real-time classes (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR, SCHED_DEADLINE) stay as fixed-priority and EDF policies above it.

code.title: CFS in miniature: smallest vruntime runs next
code.python:
# CFS in miniature: always run the task with the smallest vruntime
import heapq
NICE0 = 1024
weights = {"A": 1024, "B": 335}        # nice 0 and nice 5
vr = {n: 0.0 for n in weights}
used = {n: 0 for n in weights}
heap = [(0.0, n) for n in weights]     # stands in for the red-black tree
heapq.heapify(heap)
tick = 1                               # ms per scheduling step
for step in range(100):
    v, n = heapq.heappop(heap)         # leftmost = smallest vruntime
    used[n] += tick
    v += tick * NICE0 / weights[n]     # heavier weight -> vruntime grows slower
    heapq.heappush(heap, (v, n))
total = sum(used.values())
print("weights:", weights)
for n in weights:
    print(f"{n}: ran {used[n]} ms of {total} = {100 * used[n] / total:.1f}%"
          f" (ideal {100 * weights[n] / sum(weights.values()):.1f}%)")

followUps: CFS keeps runnable tasks in a red-black tree keyed by vruntime. Picking the next task is O(1) because the leftmost node is cached; inserting a task and removing one are O(log n). Space is O(n) for n runnable tasks, one node each. Example: with 1000 runnable tasks, each reinsert takes about 10 comparisons. Per-CPU run queues mean n is the count on one core, not the whole machine, and the tree lock is per CPU, so contention is low.

Lower its nice value so its weight is 10 times larger. Weights are about 1.25 per nice step, so you need 1.25^k = 10, which gives k near 10.3. Nice -10 against nice 0 gives 9548 / 1024, about 9.3 times; nice -11 gives about 11.6 times. Example: nice 0 and nice -10 share the CPU about 90.3% to 9.7%. Raising the other task to nice +10 also works. Only root can use negative nice values. In cgroup v2 you can set cpu.weight 1000 versus 100 instead.

EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) is the policy in Linux since 6.6. Each task has a lag, the CPU time it is owed compared with its fair share, and is eligible when lag is not negative. Among eligible tasks the scheduler runs the one with the earliest virtual deadline, which is eligible time plus slice divided by weight. A task asking for a short slice gets an earlier deadline and therefore low latency without a larger share. It was introduced because CFS needed many heuristics for latency (wake-up bonuses, granularity) that were hard to tune; EEVDF expresses latency directly.

code.title: CPU shares from nice weights

followUps: When the nice-5 task sleeps, its vruntime stops growing while others advance. On wake-up CFS sets its vruntime to max(its old vruntime, min_vruntime - a small bonus), so a long sleeper cannot return with a huge credit and monopolise the CPU. Example: the other task is at vruntime 500, the sleeper had 100; it is placed near 497 rather than 100. A short sleeper keeps its small vruntime and so tends to run almost immediately, which keeps interactive tasks responsive. It still receives its share-weight afterwards, about 25% while both are runnable.

In cgroup v2 you use cpu.weight, which ranges from 1 to 10000 with a default of 100, and it maps directly to shares between siblings. Nice does not apply between groups. For a 75/25 split give the groups cpu.weight 300 and 100. Example: echo 300 > A/cpu.weight and echo 100 > B/cpu.weight. Weights only matter when the CPU is contended; an idle CPU is used by whoever wants it. For a hard cap use cpu.max, for example 50000 100000 meaning 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period.

code.title: SRTF Gantt chart built event by event
code.python:
# SRTF Gantt chart by events: P1(0,7) P2(2,4) P3(4,1) P4(5,4)
procs = {"P1": (0, 7), "P2": (2, 4), "P3": (4, 1), "P4": (5, 4)}
rem = {n: bt for n, (at, bt) in procs.items()}
first, comp, gantt, t = {}, {}, [], 0
while len(comp) < len(procs):
    ready = [n for n, (at, _) in procs.items() if at <= t and rem[n] > 0]
    if not ready:
        t += 1; continue
    n = min(ready, key=lambda x: (rem[x], procs[x][0]))   # tie: earlier arrival
    first.setdefault(n, t)
    # run until next arrival or completion, whichever is first
    future = [at for _, (at, _) in procs.items() if at > t]
    step = min([rem[n]] + [a - t for a in future])
    if gantt and gantt[-1][0] == n: gantt[-1][2] += step
    else: gantt.append([n, t, t + step])
    t += step; rem[n] -= step
    if rem[n] == 0: comp[n] = t
for n, s, e in gantt: print(f"{n}: {s}-{e}")
tw = 0
for n, (at, bt) in procs.items():
    tat = comp[n] - at; wt = tat - bt
    tw += wt
    print(f"{n}: CT={comp[n]} TAT={tat} WT={wt} RT={first[n] - at}")
print("average WT =", tw / len(procs))

followUps: With events at 0, 2, 4, 5 and the completions, the SRTF chart is P1 0-2, P2 2-4, P3 4-5, P2 5-7, P4 7-11, P1 11-16. At 2, P2 (4) beats P1 (remaining 5); at 4, P3 (1) beats P2 (remaining 2); at 5, P2 (2) is smallest vs P4 (4) and P1 (5); P4 then P1 follow. Completion times are P1 16, P2 7, P3 5, P4 11. Waiting times: P1 9, P2 1, P3 0, P4 2, so the average is 3.0. Total slots 16 equal the sum of bursts 7+4+1+4.

The Gantt chart gets gaps or extra slots, and every metric gets worse. Each switch adds s units where nothing useful runs, so completion times shift later. Example: for the chart above with 5 switches at s=0.5, the finish moves from 16 to 18.5 and every job after a switch is delayed. Preemptive algorithms such as SRTF and RR pay for each preemption, so a small gain in average waiting can be lost. Add the switch time as its own block in the chart and state whether it counts as waiting.

code.title: Rate-Monotonic bound vs EDF schedulability
code.python:
# Real-time schedulability: Rate-Monotonic bound vs EDF bound
def rm_bound(n):
    return n * (2 ** (1 / n) - 1)

tasks = [(1, 4), (1, 5), (2, 10)]   # (compute time C, period T)
u = sum(c / t for c, t in tasks)
n = len(tasks)
print("tasks (C,T):", tasks)
print(f"utilisation U = {u:.3f}")
print(f"RM bound for n={n}: {rm_bound(n):.3f} -> ", end="")
print("guaranteed" if u <= rm_bound(n) else "not guaranteed by the bound (needs exact test)")
print("EDF bound: 1.000 -> ", "schedulable" if u <= 1 else "overloaded")
for k in (1, 2, 3, 10, 1000):
    print(f"  RM bound n={k}: {rm_bound(k):.4f}")

followUps: For three tasks the Rate-Monotonic bound is n(2^(1/n) - 1) = 3 * (2^(1/3) - 1), about 0.780. If total utilization (sum of C/T) is at most 78%, the set is guaranteed schedulable under RM. Example: tasks (1,4), (1,5), (2,10) have U = 0.25 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.65, which is under 0.78, so they are safe. Above the bound the set may still be schedulable, so use the exact response-time test. As n grows the bound falls toward ln 2, about 0.693. EDF has a bound of 1.

Linux uses scheduling classes tried in order: stop, deadline (SCHED_DEADLINE, EDF-based), real-time (SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR with priorities 1-99), fair (CFS or EEVDF for SCHED_NORMAL and SCHED_BATCH) and idle. A runnable task in a higher class always preempts a lower one. Example: a SCHED_FIFO task with priority 50 runs until it blocks or yields, ahead of every normal task. Real-time throttling (sched_rt_runtime_us, default 95%) keeps a runaway real-time task from freezing the machine. Tools: chrt sets the policy and priority.

code.title: Priority inversion with and without inheritance

followUps: With inheritance H can still be blocked for a long time by a chain of locks: if H waits for L1, which waits for a lock held by L2, and so on, H is delayed by the sum of all those critical sections. Example: three low tasks each holding a lock for 5 ms in sequence gives 15 ms of blocking. Inheritance also lets a medium-priority task inherit and the cascade lasts as long as the chain. Priority ceiling avoids chained blocking (a task can be blocked at most once by one critical section) and also avoids deadlock, at the cost of needing to know every lock's ceiling in advance.

Look for a high-priority task that is runnable-but-blocked for a long time while lower-priority tasks run. Practical signs are missed deadlines or watchdog resets, and a high wait time in run-queue latency metrics. Tools: perf sched and ftrace sched_switch events to see who ran while the high task waited, lock contention traces (lockstat, futex tracing), and eBPF tools such as offcputime. Example: H blocked 50 ms on a mutex while M ran for 48 ms is a clear inversion. Add timeouts and alerts on lock-wait time, and enable PI mutexes.

code.title: Context-switch cost versus time slice
code.python:
# Context-switch cost: useful CPU fraction for different time slices
switch_us = 5.0      # direct cost of one switch (microseconds)
cache_us = 50.0      # indirect cost: warming caches/TLB afterwards
print("slice(us)  useful%  (slice / (slice + direct + indirect))")
for slice_us in (10, 50, 100, 1000, 10000):
    useful = slice_us / (slice_us + switch_us + cache_us)
    print(f"{slice_us:9d}  {100 * useful:6.1f}")
# switches per second at a given slice and the time they eat
for slice_us in (100, 4000):
    per_sec = 1_000_000 / (slice_us + switch_us + cache_us)
    lost = per_sec * (switch_us + cache_us) / 1e6
    print(f"slice {slice_us} us: {per_sec:.0f} switches/s, {100 * lost:.1f}% of CPU lost")

followUps: A thread switch is cheaper than a process switch, because threads of one process share the same address space. Switching threads saves registers and the stack pointer only, and keeps the TLB and page tables, so cache and TLB stay warm. Switching processes also changes the page-table base, which without PCID flushes the TLB and costs further misses. Typical figures: about 1-2 microseconds for a thread switch versus 2-5 microseconds or more for a process switch, plus extra cache-miss cost afterwards. User-level threads switch in tens of nanoseconds.

In cooperative scheduling tasks yield voluntarily, usually at a point where little state is live, so there is no timer interrupt and no kernel trap. A user-space switch (goroutine, coroutine, async await) saves a few registers and swaps a stack pointer, typically 50-200 nanoseconds rather than microseconds, and there is no TLB flush. The cost is that one task that never yields blocks everything, which is the convoy problem again. Example: a server handling 100,000 requests per second with 1 microsecond kernel switches spends 10% of a core just switching; with 100 ns user switches it spends 1%.

A CPU quota (cpu.max) lets a container run for a fixed time per period, for example 50 ms in every 100 ms. Once spent, all its threads are paused until the next period even if the machine is idle. A request arriving late in the period can wait tens of milliseconds, which shows up as p99 spikes while average CPU is low. Example: a 4-thread service with a 1-CPU limit burns 40 ms of quota in 10 ms of wall time, then is frozen for 90 ms. Using requests without limits, or higher limits, avoids this. Watch nr_throttled in cpu.stat.

CPU pinning dedicates specific cores to a workload so its threads do not migrate and share caches with noisy neighbours. This keeps L1/L2 caches warm, avoids cross-NUMA memory access, and makes latency far more predictable. In Kubernetes the static CPU manager gives Guaranteed pods with integer CPU requests exclusive cores. The cost is lower overall utilization, because pinned cores cannot be used by others when idle. Example: pinning a trading process to 4 cores can cut p99 latency from 2 ms to 0.3 ms at the price of those cores.

code.title: Static vs continuous batching for LLM decoding
code.python:
# Static batching vs continuous batching for LLM decoding (iteration = 1 step)
reqs = [("A", 20), ("B", 2), ("C", 2), ("D", 2)]   # (name, tokens to generate)
SLOTS = 2                                          # batch size on the GPU

def static(rs):
    t, done, rs = 0, {}, list(rs)
    while rs:
        batch, rs = rs[:SLOTS], rs[SLOTS:]
        t += max(n for _, n in batch)             # batch ends with its slowest member
        for name, _ in batch: done[name] = t
    return done

def continuous(rs):
    t, done, waiting, active = 0, {}, list(rs), {}
    while waiting or active:
        while waiting and len(active) < SLOTS:    # refill free slots every step
            n, k = waiting.pop(0); active[n] = k
        t += 1
        for n in list(active):
            active[n] -= 1
            if active[n] == 0: del active[n]; done[n] = t
    return done

print("requests:", reqs, "slots:", SLOTS)
for title, fn in (("static", static), ("continuous", continuous)):
    d = fn(reqs)
    print(title, d, "avg finish %.1f" % (sum(d.values()) / len(d)))

followUps: Head-of-line blocking is when a request at the front of a batch or queue holds up everything behind it. In static batching a batch of 4 finishes only when its longest request ends: three 2-token replies wait for a 500-token one, so they take 500 steps instead of 2. Continuous batching removes the wait because finished sequences leave at each step and queued ones join. Long prompts cause a similar problem in prefill, since a 32k-token prefill can stall decode steps for others; chunked prefill splits it into pieces.

Use aging and a cap on preemption. Give each waiting request a priority that rises with its queue time, and never evict a request more than a set number of times. Also reserve a minimum share of batch slots or tokens per step for long-running generations, similar to a quantum guarantee in MLFQ with boosting. Example: if a long request has waited 10 seconds, add +1 priority per second so after 10 seconds it beats new short requests. Track the maximum wait and time-per-output-token as service metrics to detect starvation.
